### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.”

French

“L'homme est né libre, et partout il est dans les fers.”

The French noun is the same word for chains and for fetters; “in chains” loses that the image is specifically of slave irons.

### Attribution notes

This is the opening sentence of On the Social Contract I.1. Because it works as a standalone lament it is read as Rousseau announcing a fixed condition, whereas the sentence opens a book whose point is that the chains were made and can be unmade — the “problem” he names in I.1 is to find a legitimate form of association, not to mourn an unavoidable loss of freedom.

#### About Jean-Jacques Rousseau

Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was a Genevan-born philosopher and novelist of the French Enlightenment who unsettled its confidence in progress. Discourses on inequality and the arts, Émile, and The Social Contract made him famous and persecuted.

### Interpretation

The opening line of The Social Contract states the problem the book tries to solve rather than a conclusion. "Born free" describes a state prior to lawful authority; "everywhere in chains" describes the actual condition of people under existing governments. The question Rousseau then asks is what could make obedience legitimate rather than merely habitual. The line is often quoted as a defence of rebellion, but the book is equally suspicious of mere force and spends most of its argument trying to identify authority a person could rationally consent to.

#### Why it matters

The persistent question is not whether constraints exist — they always do — but which ones you could endorse on reflection. That reframing separates the useful complaint from the merely resentful one.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Man is born free, and everywhere he is…”?

“Man is born free, and everywhere he is…” comes from The Social Contract, Book I, Ch., 1, attributed to Jean-Jacques Rousseau.

#### What does Jean-Jacques Rousseau mean by freedom?

Philosophers distinguish several ideas under the single word freedom. Negative freedom emphasizes non-interference; positive freedom emphasizes the capacity to act according to reasons, virtue, or authentic desire. This passage enters that discussion through freedom, society, awakening.

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

This is the opening sentence of On the Social Contract I.1. Because it works as a standalone lament it is read as Rousseau announcing a fixed condition, whereas the sentence opens a book whose point is that the chains were made and can be unmade — the “problem” he names in I.1 is to find a legitimate form of association, not to mourn an unavoidable loss of freedom.
